note: Feedback for the Checks of Unit 6, read from the lesson files, where it was written with the lessons (docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-27-chemstudy-unit-6-lessons-design.md). The option with no message is the answer. tests/e2e/check-feedback.spec.ts compares each lesson page with this file.

options.text: Wet concrete (the system) warming the wooden forms around it as it cures
options.message: The forms are surroundings, and they warm. Which way did energy go between them and the concrete?

options.text: A pat of butter (the system) melting in a warm pan
A baked loaf of bread (the system) cooling on a rack
options.message: As the loaf's temperature falls, is its own energy rising or falling? Endothermic means the system's energy rises.

options.text: Water vapor (the system) turning to frost on a cold windshield
options.message: Compare the vapor with the frost. In which are the molecules held more firmly? Settling into attractions releases energy.

options.text: The wax takes in energy from the hand as it hardens, so hardening is endothermic for the wax.
options.message: If the wax took energy from the hand, would the hand feel warm or cool? Check the direction against what the patient feels.

options.text: The wax keeps getting hotter while it hardens, so it has more and more energy to pass on to the hand.
options.message: Nothing is heating the wax once the hand leaves the bath. Ask what happens to a liquid's energy as it becomes a solid.

options.text: The hand is warmer than the room, so it supplies the energy that turns the liquid wax into a solid.
options.message: The hand ends up warmer, not cooler, so it was not the supplier. Which way did energy cross between the wax and the hand?

options.text: Hardening is exothermic for the wax: its energy falls, and the hand gains the energy it gives up.
The iron and oxygen released energy as they reacted, and the thermometer gained it: exothermic.
Oxygen gas is warmer than nitrogen gas, so letting the air in is what warmed the thermometer's bulb.
options.message: Both gases came from the same room at 21 °C. What can oxygen do with iron that nitrogen cannot?

options.text: Traces of vinegar on the steel wool warmed the thermometer, and the gas in the jar played no part.
options.message: The vinegar was on the wool the whole time. Did the reading move while the jar held only nitrogen?

options.text: The reaction took energy in from the thermometer, and a thermometer shows that as a higher reading.
options.message: A thermometer that loses energy cools, and its reading falls. Which way did this reading go?

options.text: The attractions between the ions in solid potassium chloride are too weak to matter.
options.message: Ions in a crystal attract one another strongly (topic 2.3). Compare the energy taken in with the energy released.

options.text: Forming attractions between ions and water released more energy than pulling particles apart took.
options.message: If more energy were released than taken in, the extra would go into the water. Does that match the reading?

options.text: Pulling the particles apart took more energy than the new ion–water attractions released.
No attractions formed between the ions and the water molecules, so no energy was released at all.
options.message: The salt dissolved, so ions and water molecules do attract (topic 3.10). How does what that released compare with what was needed?

options.text: Its energy rose by 950 J, so the dissolving is endothermic.
options.message: The water is surroundings, and it gained the 950 J. Can the system and the surroundings both gain energy?

options.text: Its energy fell by 950 J, so the dissolving is exothermic.
Its energy did not change, because energy is conserved.
options.message: Conserved means the total for system plus surroundings stays constant. Either part can change if the other changes the opposite way.

options.text: Its energy fell by more than 950 J, because warming the water used up extra energy on top of that.
options.message: Warming the water is where the 950 J went. With no energy passing to the cup or the air, where could any extra have gone?

options.text: A rise, because the products have 80 kJ more energy to pass on to the water.
options.message: Check which side ends with more energy. Can the system gain 80 kJ and also hand 80 kJ to the water?

options.text: A rise, because a reaction releases the amount of energy shown by the gap.
options.message: A gap can be energy released or energy absorbed. Which way does the arrow run when the products' level is the higher one?

options.text: A fall, because the system takes the energy it gains from the water.
No change, because energy is conserved and the two levels cancel out.
options.message: Conservation covers the system and the surroundings together. The system's own energy changes by the gap between the levels.

slips.message: Did you leave off the sign, or take starting minus final? A change is final minus starting.
Did you add the two levels? A change is the final level minus the starting level.
Is that the two levels added? The gap between them is the final level minus the starting level.

options.text: Liquid tin on the upper level, solid tin on the lower level, and the arrow pointing down
Solid tin on the upper level, liquid tin on the lower level, and the arrow pointing down
options.message: An arrow runs from the start to the finish. Follow this one: which form of tin does it start from?

options.text: Liquid tin on the lower level, solid tin on the upper level, and the arrow pointing up
options.message: This has the tin gaining energy as it hardens. Topic 6.1 put freezing among the exothermic changes. Does the system's energy rise or fall?

options.text: Liquid tin and solid tin on one level, because the temperature stays at 232 °C throughout
options.message: A steady temperature does not mean a steady energy. Energy still leaves the tin as it hardens.

options.text: Levels at 25 and 140 kJ/mol, with the arrow pointing up: 115 kJ/mol absorbed
options.message: 140 kJ/mol is the top of the hill. An energy diagram keeps the start and the finish. Which two numbers are those?

options.text: Levels at 140 and 70 kJ/mol, with the arrow pointing down: 70 kJ/mol released
options.message: A diagram of a change begins at the level where the change begins. Where do the reactants sit on this profile?

options.text: Levels at 25 and 70 kJ/mol, with the arrow pointing down: 45 kJ/mol released
options.message: A change runs from its starting level to its final level. Which level of this profile is the start, and is the finish above it or below it?

options.text: Levels at 25 and 70 kJ/mol, with the arrow pointing up: 45 kJ/mol absorbed
The reaction is fast, because the drop in energy is large.
options.message: The size of the drop is an amount of energy. What on a profile from topic 5.6 decides how fast a reaction goes?

options.text: The system releases 200 kJ to its surroundings as the reaction happens.
The reaction needs no energy to get it started, because it runs downhill.
options.message: Burning paper runs downhill too, yet a sheet can sit in air for years (topic 5.6). Is the hill drawn on this diagram?

options.text: The products end up colder than the reactants were, because they have less energy.
options.message: The levels show the system's energy, not a temperature. A lower level does not say that the products are cold.

options.text: The oil's is greater, because the particles of a liquid are free to move around.
options.message: Free to move around is about how the particles are arranged. What does the temperature of a body measure?

options.text: The glass's is zero, because particles that are held in place in a solid do not move.
options.message: Particles in a solid vibrate about fixed positions (topic 3.5), and that motion is kinetic energy.

options.text: Whichever of the two has the greater mass, the oil or the bottle, has the greater average.
options.message: An average is per particle. Would pouring more oil into the bottle change the temperature of the oil?

options.text: They are equal, because the oil and the glass are at the same temperature.
Cold flows out of the can into the skin until the skin's particles have slowed down.
options.message: Nothing called cold travels. Ask what the particles on each side of the surface are doing, and which have more kinetic energy.

options.text: Particles of the skin collide with particles of the can and, on balance, pass kinetic energy to them.
Fast particles leave the skin and move into the can's wall, carrying their kinetic energy across with them.
options.message: Skin does not move into aluminum. Energy can cross a surface without any particle crossing it. How?

options.text: Collisions swap energy back and forth until the hand and the can each hold the same total amount of energy.
options.message: Check the stopping point. A hand and a can are different sizes. What has to match for the net transfer to stop?

options.text: Energy still passes both ways between probe and meat in collisions, in equal amounts.
Collisions between the particles of the probe and the particles of the meat have stopped.
options.message: Particles at 74 °C are still moving, so they still collide. A steady reading needs something less drastic.

options.text: The probe and the chicken now hold equal amounts of energy, which keeps the reading steady.
options.message: A small probe and a whole chicken are at one temperature. Compare how many particles each has. Can their total energies match?

options.text: The particles of the steel probe now move at the same average speed as the particles of the meat.
options.message: Equal temperatures mean equal average kinetic energies. Iron atoms and water molecules differ in mass, so what follows for speed?

options.text: From the lake to the swimmer, because the lake holds far more energy in total.
options.message: The total depends on how much water there is. Does a lake's size decide how hard each molecule hits the swimmer's skin?

options.text: Neither way, because a lake is far too large for one swimmer to change its temperature.
options.message: A change too small to measure is still a transfer. Can 33 °C skin touch 18 °C water with no net flow of energy?

options.text: From the swimmer to the lake, because the skin's particles have the greater average kinetic energy.
Both ways in equal amounts from the first moment, because collisions pass energy in both directions.
options.message: Equal amounts both ways describes thermal equilibrium. Are the swimmer and the lake at the same temperature yet?

options.text: The glass cools and the juice warms until they share one temperature between 6 °C and 60 °C.
The glass cools to 6 °C while the juice stays at 6 °C, because a cold liquid holds its temperature.
options.message: The energy the glass loses has to go somewhere. What happens to the juice's particles as more energetic ones keep striking them?

options.text: Both end at exactly 33 °C, because thermal equilibrium is always halfway between the starting temperatures.
options.message: Halfway is a special case. A thin glass and a lot of juice need not change by the same number of degrees.

options.text: The glass cools and the juice warms until each holds the same amount of energy, at two different temperatures.
options.message: What two bodies share at thermal equilibrium is the thing a thermometer reads. Is that their total energy?
